title: Delhi High Court Division Bench Upholds Setting Aside of Termination Payment in NHAI Highway Arbitration
meta_description: Delhi High Court Division Bench affirms a tribunal cannot compute NHAI termination payment using a cost figure exceeding the contract's defined ceiling.
bench: Division Bench (names not independently confirmed across sources)
case_name: National Highways Authority of India v. M/S Kurukshetra Expressway Private Limited
body: Road concession contracts in India are drafted with elaborate formulas for what a terminated concessionaire is owed, precisely so that a dispute over termination does not turn into an open-ended valuation exercise years later. A Division Bench of the Delhi High Court has now reminded an arbitral tribunal, and through it the wider infrastructure bar, that those formulas mean what they say even when a tribunal finds a more generous figure elsewhere in the record.

The dispute arose out of a highway concession awarded to Kurukshetra Expressway Private Limited, a joint venture in which Kalpataru Projects International holds a 49.57 per cent stake, which NHAI terminated in 2021. The arbitral tribunal that heard KEPL's claims awarded it a termination payment computed using a project cost figure of approximately ₹1,045.55 crore, drawn from what the parties referred to as a Disaggregation Letter submitted during the project's execution. NHAI challenged the award under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, and a single judge of the Delhi High Court, by order dated 28 July 2026, partly allowed that challenge, setting aside the termination payment and the interest awarded on it while leaving every other head of claim in the award undisturbed.

A mismatch between the figure the tribunal used and the figure the contract itself prescribes lies at the heart of the single judge's reasoning, which the Division Bench has now affirmed. Article 48.1 of the concession agreement defines Total Project Cost in terms that cap it at ₹650 crore, a ceiling considerably below the ₹1,045.55 crore the tribunal had worked with. A tribunal computing termination payment is not free to substitute a higher figure drawn from subsequent project correspondence for the figure the parties contractually agreed would govern that calculation, however persuasive the later document might otherwise appear.

NHAI's appeal under Section 37 against the partial setting-aside went nowhere before the Division Bench, which upheld the single judge's order on 28 September 2026. The Bench's reasoning, as reported, rested on a point of construction that arbitration practitioners will recognise as settled law stated with unusual bluntness: where a contract inserts words of limitation defining or capping a figure central to a dispute, a court cannot treat those words as surplus. The parties did not include a Total Project Cost definition with a stated ceiling by accident, and a tribunal's award that quietly overrides that ceiling by reference to an informal letter exceeds the kind of contractual interpretation Section 34 permits an arbitrator to make.

The amount at stake gives the ruling its commercial weight. KEPL's termination payment claim, before the Division Bench's affirmance, had been reported in the range of ₹911 crore, a figure that would have made this one of the larger arbitral awards against NHAI to survive judicial scrutiny intact had the single judge not intervened. With both the single judge's order and now the Division Bench's affirmance going against KEPL on this specific head, the joint venture is left with the awards on its other claims, which were never disturbed, but loses the termination payment component that formed the bulk of the overall award's value.

Kalpataru Projects International's own disclosure to the stock exchanges, filed within hours of receiving the Division Bench's order, signalled that the fight is not over. The company said KEPL believes it has a strong case and is taking appropriate legal steps, language that in the context of an NHAI arbitration almost certainly points toward a further appeal, whether by special leave to the Supreme Court or by some other route available once the High Court's remedies are exhausted. The underlying claims on other heads remain intact regardless of how that further round plays out, since the Division Bench's order touched only the termination payment and interest.

For infrastructure lawyers advising on highway and other PPP concessions, the case is a cautionary note on how tightly a tribunal's termination payment calculation must track the contract's own defined cost figures. A Disaggregation Letter, cost escalation correspondence, or any other document generated during project execution may well reflect the economic reality of what a project actually cost to build, but if the concession agreement has already fixed a ceiling for the purpose of calculating termination payment, that ceiling controls the calculation regardless of what later correspondence says the real number was. Drafters negotiating these ceilings at the outset should treat them as more than a formality, since a generation of commercial escalation can leave a concessionaire arguing, as KEPL did here, that the contractual figure is now badly out of step with reality, only to find the courts unwilling to let the tribunal correct that gap on its own.
why_it_matters: Concessionaires and authorities negotiating termination payment clauses in highway and other PPP concessions should treat the contractually defined cost ceiling as binding for the life of the project, since courts will set aside an arbitral award that computes termination payment using a higher figure drawn from later project correspondence, even where that figure may better reflect actual project cost. Tribunals deciding termination disputes must anchor their calculations to the contract's own defined terms rather than supplementary documents generated during execution.
card_summary: Delhi High Court Division Bench upholds setting aside of a large termination payment award against NHAI, since the tribunal used a project cost figure exceeding the concession's defined ceiling.
card_tip: When drafting termination payment formulas in PPP concessions, set a realistic project cost ceiling; tribunals cannot override it using later correspondence.
verification_notes: The 28 July 2026 single judge order and the 28 September 2026 Division Bench order upholding it are confirmed by Kalpataru Projects International's own NSE regulatory filing (a near-primary source) together with PSU Connect, LiveLawBiz and ScanX reporting. The ₹650 crore contractual ceiling under Article 48.1 and the ₹1,045.55 crore Disaggregation Letter figure are confirmed by LiveLawBiz's detailed report. The termination payment figure is reported as approximately ₹911 crore across LiveLawBiz headlines; this is stated as a reported range rather than a court-confirmed figure. The Division Bench's judges' names were given in only one unverified source and are deliberately omitted here rather than stated without a second confirming source. KEPL's stated intention to pursue further legal steps is drawn directly from the company's own exchange disclosure.
